appraisal_events.evidence: « — Quoi ? demanda d'une voix forte mon grand-père qui était devenu un peu sourd et qui n'avait pas entendu quelque chose que mon cousin venait de dire à mon père. — Rien, répondit le cousin. »
appraisal_events.explanation: The grandfather is staged as outside the exchange: deaf, forced to ask loudly, and then put off with « Rien » and a substituted banality about the weather, which the father takes up over his head. The narrator's gloss on his deafness makes the diminishment part of the telling rather than merely of the dialogue.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Promettez-moi que vous ne viendrez pas “demain”. Faites-le pour “elle”. […] Elle vous avait demandé de ne pas venir. » / « Rien n'y faisait ; il était toujours le premier à la “maison” »
appraisal_events.explanation: The mother's earnest plea, made on the dying grandmother's behalf, is answered by a flat statement of its total futility: her appeal carries no weight against the cousin's habitual intrusion. The irony falls mainly on the cousin, but the local movement leaves her request disregarded.

status_effects.explanation: He is locally shut out of the conversation his son and the cousin are conducting, and is given a deflecting non-answer rather than being included.
Her direct, repeated entreaty produces no effect at all (« Rien n'y faisait »), so her speech is locally shown to have no purchase.

ambiguities: The passage's principal evaluative target is the unnamed « mon cousin », whom the narrator plainly ironizes (the nickname « ni fleurs ni couronnes », the tag « Vous, on ne vous dit pas merci »); scope rules exclude unnamed figures not on the reference sheet, so that dominant irony is recorded only through its second-order effects on the named family members.

It is underdetermined whether the grandfather's exclusion is an intentional brush-off by the cousin or merely the incidental consequence of his deafness, and whether the party who nullifies maman's plea is the cousin specifically or the generalized social custom the narrator describes in habitual mode (« il était toujours le premier »).
